[t09] The Reverse Priority Thesis: Discontinuous Promising Is the Paradigm
Thesis: The practice of promising is functionally designed for securing future performance from agents whose motivational states cannot be relied upon to persist. Promising across psychological discontinuity is therefore the central case, and ordinary individual promising is a limiting case in which continuity happens to make the institutional supports redundant.
Argument sketch: Hume's account of promising as an artificial virtue explains promises as a remedy for the unreliability of future motivation. Discontinuity is the extreme of that unreliability. If promising's function is to bind an agent whose future self may not share present intentions, then the cases where the future stage shares nothing are where the function is most fully exercised, not where it fails. Corporate and treaty commitments, which outlive all their makers, are historically and structurally central to the practice of binding commitments. Theories that make personal identity a precondition of promising thus mistake an incidental feature of the simplest case for an essential feature of the practice. I show that practice-based accounts (Rawls, Kolodny and Wallace) are best read this way, and that this reading answers Owens's objection that practice views cannot explain bare promises.
What it adds: The literature treats corporate and AI promising as derivative extensions to be explained by analogy with individual promising. This thesis inverts that priority on functional and genealogical grounds and draws the consequences for the debate between conventionalist and non-conventionalist theories of promising.

[t17] Content-Relative Continuity
Thesis: What a promise requires of the performing stage is not global psychological continuity with the promising stage but continuity of the specific capacities and attitudes the promised performance draws on. Promissory binding is therefore relative to content.
Argument sketch: A promise to repay money can be kept by a stage with almost no psychological connection to the promiser, provided it controls the relevant funds. A promise to remain faithful to a lover requires continuity of the attitudes that constitute fidelity, and cannot be honored by a stage that lacks them, however continuous it is otherwise. Parfit's view that what matters is Relation R is too coarse, because it treats all psychological connections as equally relevant to all obligations. I argue that the promise's content determines which connections are relevant. This explains why a demented patient may still be bound by a financial commitment but not a relational one, why an AI instance may be bound to a factual task but not to an expressive commitment, and why corporate commitments survive turnover while those dependent on particular individuals do not.
What it adds: Parfitian reductionism makes identity-relevant connections uniform across obligations. Identity-based views make identity all-or-nothing. This thesis introduces a third option, binding relative to the performance-relevant connections, which yields differentiated verdicts within each case type. Neither position in the existing literature captures that differentiation.

[t15] Discontinuity as a Crucial Test: Authority Theories Beat Expectation Theories
Thesis: Promises across psychological discontinuity are a crucial test case that discriminates between theories of promissory obligation. Expectation-based theories (Scanlon's Principle F) cannot explain why such promises bind, and authority-based theories (Owens) can.
Argument sketch: On expectation views, the duty is owed by whoever voluntarily and intentionally led the promisee to expect performance. In discontinuity cases, that agent no longer exists at performance time, so the theory can locate the wrong only in the earlier stage's act of inducing expectation. That collapses promissory obligation into a duty of care in assertion. Authority views ground the obligation in the promisee's interest in having authority over the promisor's conduct. That authority is a property of the promisee's normative position, which persists, and can therefore attach to whatever agent occupies the promised role. I show that the authority view correctly predicts that promisees retain claims against corporate successors and AI deployments. The expectation view predicts only claims against past agents, which are often unreachable. The discontinuity cases are thus evidence for the authority view, which has struggled to find decisive support.
What it adds: Debates between Scanlonian and Owensian theories have been conducted using ordinary cases in which both theories agree. This thesis identifies a class of cases in which they diverge in their predictions and argues that intuitive verdicts favor one side, providing new evidence in a long-running dispute.

[t08] The Appropriation Condition: Why the AI Case and the Dementia Case Come Apart
Thesis: A later stage is bound by an earlier stage's promise if and only if it has the capacity, at performance time, to take the promise as a reason of its own when presented with it. That capacity can be present without memory (memoryless AI) and absent despite continuity of organism (advanced dementia).
Argument sketch: Promissory obligation functions as a reason-giving relation: its point is that the promisor treats the promisee's claim as settling what to do. A stage that cannot so treat the claim cannot be bound in the relevant sense, because the obligation would be idle. A stage that can, when informed, is apt to be bound, since being given the record of one's commitment and recognizing it as a valid claim is how normative uptake works. A memoryless AI instance presented with a transcript can appropriate. A patient with advanced dementia often cannot, even with full narrative support. Hence the three standard cases sort differently than continuity theories predict, and the sorting matches considered judgments.
What it adds: Jaworska's work on 'valuing' at the margins of agency addresses whether dementia patients retain agency, but not what that implies for prior commitments. Narrative views require self-interpretation over time. This thesis proposes a synchronic, capacity-based criterion that is externally triggerable, and argues that it, rather than any diachronic relation, is what promissory binding requires.

[t12] Advance Directives as Promises to Third Parties
Thesis: Advance directives for dementia do not bind the later self through precedent autonomy. They bind as promises made to carers and family, so the power to release the directive lies with those promisees and not with the demented patient.
Argument sketch: Dworkin grounds directives in the patient's critical interests, and Dresser objects that the later self's welfare should govern. Both treat the directive as a matter between the earlier and the later self. But directives are typically addressed to others: 'Do not keep me alive if…'. They thus have the structure of a promise, or of an authorization creating claims in third parties. If so, the classic promissory rule applies: the promisee, not the promisor, holds the power to release. This explains a widely shared intuition that neither side of the Dworkin–Dresser debate can account for, namely that carers may sometimes justifiably depart from a directive. The departure is a release exercised by the promisees, not a betrayal of the patient. The thesis also yields limits: carers may release only within the scope of the original grant, and may not release in ways that serve their own interests at the patient's expense.
What it adds: This recasts the precedent-autonomy debate in the vocabulary of directed promissory obligation. It identifies who holds the release power and why, and it resolves a stalemate in bioethics by locating the decisive normative power in a third party rather than in either self.

[t18] Branching Promisors Owe Jointly, Not Severally
Thesis: When a promising agent branches into multiple discontinuous successors, as when a conversational AI is instantiated in many parallel sessions or a corporation splits, the promise binds the branches jointly and not each branch severally. The obligation is collective and is discharged when any branch performs.
Argument sketch: Parfit's fission cases suggest that if identity is not what matters, both fission products inherit whatever matters, including obligations. But if each branch were severally bound, a single promise would multiply into many obligations, which is absurd: one promise to pay $100 cannot create a debt of $100 per instance. The resulting structure is that of joint obligation, familiar from law: each branch is answerable, but performance by one discharges all. I show that this structure follows from the promisee's interest, which is in one performance, not many. Collective-obligation theory (Collins, Björnsson) supplies the account of how unstructured groups can hold such duties. The view also yields distinctive verdicts about blame: no single branch is blameworthy for collective non-performance unless it could have performed.
What it adds: Fission cases in personal-identity theory have been used to test theories of prudential concern, not of obligation. This thesis applies them to promissory obligation, identifies a multiplication problem the existing literature has missed, and resolves it with the joint/several distinction from law and collective-obligation theory.

[t16] Discontinuity Dissolves the Paradox of Self-Promising
Thesis: The standard objection to promises to oneself, that the promisee can always release the promisor and so no binding occurs, fails when promisor and promisee are psychologically discontinuous stages. Discontinuous agents can therefore make genuinely binding self-promises in a way continuous agents cannot.
Argument sketch: Hobbes, and later Habib, argued that self-promises are empty because the person who is bound is also the person with power to release. When the earlier stage promises the later stage, however, and the two lack psychological continuity, they do not share the same will. The later stage holds the release power and the earlier stage holds the obligation, or vice versa, and these are not exercised by a single will. So the release objection loses its force. This yields a counterintuitive result: an agent anticipating dementia may make a promise to her future self, and that promise may bind her pre-dementia stage in a way an ordinary self-promise could not. It also clarifies what self-promising theorists like Rosati were reaching for.
What it adds: Defenses of self-promising (Rosati, Habib) try to answer the release objection within a single continuous self. This thesis argues that the objection is decisive for continuous selves but inapplicable across discontinuity. It thereby relocates the conditions for genuine self-promising and links two literatures, self-promising and personal identity, that have developed separately.
